learner._comment: What the learner is CALLED, in the definite form the instructions and the panel use: "the pupil", "the student", "the participant" or anything else. A tree sets it with the config row `learner`, as free text; left out, `default` applies. `legacy` maps the keys trees used before 0.31.0 (`pupil`, `student`, `participant`) to that form, so an older file reads the same. `leadIn` is what the panel prints in front of a description; {LearnerDefinite} is the form with a capital first letter. A skill is a verb phrase ("The student can: add ..."), a concept a definition, and they need different lead-ins.

help.label: How do I use this page?
help.heading: How do I use this page?

sections.heading: The menu button
sections.body: Press the ☰ button at the bottom left, next to this help button, to open a menu with the back link, light/dark mode, your progress and the other buttons on the page — explained below.

sections.heading: The map
sections.body: The map shows how learning goals build on one another, from the most basic at the top to the most composite at the bottom. Boxes you do not have the prerequisites for yet appear grey and locked — tick off the ones you are missing first. Drag to pan the map, and use +/- or the mouse wheel to zoom.

sections.heading: Click a box
sections.body: When you click a box you get the prerequisites, a full description of the learning goal, and an AI instruction you can copy and paste into an AI chat to practise that particular learning goal. Mark the box as mastered when you know it — your progress is saved in your browser, and you can remove the mark again whenever you like.

sections.heading: “Show all learning goals”
sections.body: This button gives you a single systematic list of every learning goal in the course, sorted by topic — useful when you want an overview or want to read the whole list without clicking through the map. Each goal shows its status: ✓ means you have marked it as mastered, ◇ means you have everything you need to learn it now, and ⊘ shows which goals you should take first (with their code, e.g. C1). You can tick goals as mastered straight from the list, in order, instead of finding each node in the map.

sections.heading: “Search”
sections.body: The search looks in the name, the description and the topic of every learning goal, and marks where the word occurs. It is the quickest way into the map when you remember a word from a learning goal but not which topic it sits under. Click a result to go to the node.

sections.heading: “Lesson planner” (for teachers)
sections.body: In the lesson planner, teachers can tick the learning goals the next lesson should cover, set the length of the lesson, and get an AI instruction for a complete lesson plan: a starter, a walkthrough using the example-problem pair model, diagnostic questions and retrieval practice at the end. The mastery ticks are your own, in your own browser — they show what you personally have been through, not what the class actually knows.

sections.heading: “Make a test from mastered learning goals”
sections.body: This button gives you an AI instruction for a test covering a selection of what you have already marked as mastered. Paste it into an AI chat to test yourself across several learning goals at once.

sections.heading: The aid tag
sections.body: The tag on a box shows which aid level the learning goal belongs to — for example "Part 1" or "Part 2". If it is split into several colours, the learning goal belongs to several levels, and you should be able to manage it under the most restrictive one. Click the tag to open "About the course", where each level is explained.

sections.heading: “Why should I learn this?”
sections.body: This button gives you an AI instruction for a short conversation about why the subject is worth learning at all. Paste it into an AI chat if you need a nudge in the right direction.

safety.label: Safety
safety.heading: Safety
safety.lead: A skill tree is made by a teacher, but anyone can make a file that looks like one. Read this before you use a tree someone has sent you.

sections.heading: A skill tree never asks for personal details
sections.body: The tree has no login and needs nothing about you. It never asks for your name, a password, your school login, an ID number, your address, your phone number or which school you go to. Your progress is stored only in the browser on this device. If a page that looks like a skill tree asks for any of this, it is not genuine. Close it, and tell your teacher.

sections.heading: Who sent you the tree?
sections.body: The most important question is where the tree came from. A tree on aiskilltrees.com, or one your teacher has posted where you usually get your course material, you can trust as much as you trust your teacher. If you got a file by email, in a chat or on social media from someone you do not know, or it arrived unexpectedly, be sceptical, even if it looks right.

sections.heading: An HTML file is a web page, not a document
sections.body: When a tree is shared as an .html file, you are not getting a document like a PDF or a Word file. You are getting a whole web page with code that runs when you open it. The browser stops it from reading your files or installing anything on the computer, but it can show anything at all: a fake login page, a button that downloads something, or links on to other websites. Whoever made the file decides what it does. Looking like a skill tree does not make it one. Never log in or download anything from a page you opened from a file.

sections.heading: Check links before you click
sections.body: The resources in the tree can link to videos, exercises and textbooks. Hover over a link, or press and hold it, and see where it goes before you click. If you do not recognise the website, or the address looks odd, leave it.

sections.heading: Instructions can be tampered with
sections.body: The AI instruction you copy is text written by whoever made the tree, and you paste it straight into an AI chat. Whoever makes a tree can write anything in it, including orders that make the chat behave differently from what you expect: give you wrong answers, send you to another website or ask about things that are none of its business. This is called prompt injection. You may want to skim the text before you paste it, and you should not trust the chat blindly.

sections.heading: You decide what you tell the chat
sections.body: Some instructions ask the chat to get to know you, for example how you feel about the subject and what you are good at. You can answer as much or as little as you like. But no instruction needs your name, contact details or passwords. If the chat asks for anything like that, do not answer, and tell your teacher. Remember too that what you write in an AI chat is stored by the company that runs the chat. Your school often has access to an AI service where your privacy is protected. Ask your teacher, and use it if you have one.

sections.heading: For teachers: a tree from a colleague
sections.body: If you received a tree from someone else, you can open it in the builder at aiskilltrees.com/make-your-own/ before you share it with your students, to be sure. The builder only takes the spreadsheet out of the file and makes a new, clean file from it, and there you can read every instruction the tree uses.

prompt._comment: The fallback language layer. A tree whose language has no languages/<code>.json yet falls back to this file for the UI, but NOT for outputLanguage — the engine generates that from the tree's own `language` field, so a German tree converses in German on day one with no translation work. `writingStyle` holds one English example of the active-voice advice (Vidar, 2026-10-03: it should not be empty). Because this file also serves every language that has no file of its own, the example says to apply the same idea in the conversation language. The language-independent half of that advice is NOT missing — it lives in prompts/shared.json → writingStyleGeneral and applies to every tree regardless. NOTE: `outputLanguage` says which language the conversation STARTS in — it must not forbid the student from asking for another one. The student's right to ask for a different language, and what happens when they do, is language-independent and lives in prompts/shared.json → languageSwitch. Do not write an absolute prohibition here: the two would contradict each other, and the model follows the prohibition.
prompt.outputLanguage: Conduct the conversation in {conversationLanguage}: the skill tree below is written in it, and the user expects it. Do not switch language on your own initiative or comment on the language of these instructions. Address the user as "you"; where the learner must be named, the word is “{learnerDefinite}”.
prompt.writingStyle:
An example in English of the first piece of advice above (in another conversation language, apply the same idea in that language):
- Active voice: write "we can write the number as …", not "the number can only be written as …"; write "we do this by …" or "you do this by …", not "this is done by …". Avoid "is done" and "can be done" where you can say who does it.
